name: JNJ-26146900

lead: JNJ-26146900 is an experimental SARM that Johnson & Johnson studied as a possible prostate cancer drug. It was never marketed.
In rats it shrank prostate tumors and limited castration-related bone loss. No human trials have been published, and nothing is known about any muscle or appearance effect in people.

paras: It binds the androgen receptor and acts differently in different tissues: antagonist-like in the prostate, with anabolic effects reported in muscle and bone in animals.
Human safety has not been studied. It is not approved for any use.

studies.source: The Journal of steroid biochemistry and molecular biology

lead: JNJ-26146900 is an experimental nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) developed by Johnson & Johnson, investigated as a possible prostate cancer treatment. It has never been marketed and, according to Wikipedia, was never tested in humans.[1]

In a 2007 rat study, the compound bound the androgen receptor with modest affinity and behaved as an antagonist in a cell-based assay, similar to bicalutamide, while showing tissue-selective effects in animals: it reduced prostate weight and prostate tumor size and prevented some of the bone loss that follows castration.[2] Because it is a SARM-class research compound, it is occasionally mentioned in muscle-building discussions, but no human appearance or muscle data exist.

paras: In the original characterisation, JNJ-26146900 bound the rat androgen receptor with a Ki of about 400 nM and acted as a pure antagonist in an in vitro cell-based assay, resembling bicalutamide in that setting.[2] In intact and castrated rats it reduced ventral prostate weight and slowed growth of prostate tumors, and it limited bone loss after orchidectomy.[2]
Wikipedia describes the profile as agonist-like in muscle and bone and antagonist-like in the prostate, and notes it is structurally related to JNJ-37654032.[1]
No studies found. The only published work is preclinical research in rats.[2]
The compound has no approved use anywhere and was not developed as a cosmetic or performance product. Its appearance in lists of SARMs reflects its class rather than any documented human use.

timeline.event: Pharmacological activity in rats described in the scientific literature.[2]
